messages.author: 62a7fe14c0ce6d79
messages.subject: phylo.modularity
parts:
Hi all
I have a dataset of 53 cranial landmarks of mammalian crania on which I'm testing 5 different possible modularity schemes.
Using the regular modularity.test indicates that all 5 schemes are significantly different from null (p = 0.001), with CR values between 0.66 and 0.82, and Z values ranging from -3 to -6. Presumably the scheme with the most negative Z score is preferred.

However using the phylo.modularity function indicates that none of these 5 schemes are significant (p ranging from 0.08 to 1), with CR values 0.92 to 1.35, and Z values from -1.5 to +5.5

The differences in result are quite striking, but I'm not sure how to interpret this. It's often the case that comparisons within a phylogenetic context are to be preferred, but I can't find examples of others using this specific phylogenetic modularity test.

I also tried running modularity.test on the phylogenetically independent contrasts of my procrustes-transformed landmark dataset. The results are closer to the non-phylogenetic modularity test (and this makes sense to me).

Any thoughts on why the phylo.modularity function produces such different results than a PIC approach?

Thanks

Faysal

messages.author: 4d71c6e24fb21497
messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] phylo.modularity
parts:
If I can rephrase your question, you are asking why you have one result when ignoring phylogenetic nonindependence and get a different result when phylogeny is taken into account.  This can happen, and is particularly acute in datasets where interspecific trends also covary with phylogenetic relatedness. When this happens, phylogeny has confounded the signal, and an analysis ignoring phylogeny is incorrect.

 

I suggest a careful reading of the basic statistical literature on phylogenetic comparative methods, starting with Felsenstein 1985 (Am Nat). Recent reviews of PCMs for morphometric data (e.g., Adams and Collyer 2019: Ann. Rev.; 2018: Syst. Biol.) have additional references.

 

Dr. Dean C. Adams

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] phylo.modularity
parts:
Thanks for the response, but I’m aware of PCMs, and my question was more specifically about the phylo.modularity function.

Let me try this a different way: why might the results using phylo.modularity differ significantly from an approach using PIC?

Below is an example using the attached testdata.Rdata file. Results for non-phylogenetic and PIC of landmark data are similar (modularity present, p=0.001) while the phylo.modularity test indicates it is not (p=1, CR>1).

Adams & Felice 2014 discusses some differences between PIC vs PGLS evolutionary covariance matrix approaches, but can this produce such different results on the same dataset?
Perhaps I’m missing something obvious here…?

Thanks again.

##
library(geomorph)
library(ape)

coords.test <- test.data$coords.test #53 3D landmarks, 10 species
partitions <- test.data$partitions #partition scheme with 6 modules
tree <- test.data$tree

# Non-phylogenetic modularity test
non.ph.mod <- modularity.test(coords.test, partition.gp=partitions)

# Phylogenetic modularity test
ph.mod <- phylo.modularity(coords.test, partition.gp=partitions, phy=tree, CI = FALSE, iter=499)

# PIC modularity test
coords.2d <- two.d.array(coords.test)
pic.mat <- apply(coords.2d, 2, pic, phy=tree) #PIC landmark matrix
pic.mat <- arrayspecs(pic.mat, 53,3)
pic.mod <- modularity.test(pic.mat, partition.gp=partitions)

# Compare results
cbind(non.ph.mod, pic.mod, ph.mod)

##

messages.author: 4d71c6e24fb21497
messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] phylo.modularity
parts:
See Adams and Collyer 2015 Evolution (the ‘what you shuffles matters’ paper). Shuffling PICs is not correct for linear models, and is correct here. They are not the correct exchangeable units under the null hypothesis (see Commanges 2003 for general comments on exchangeability for permutation tests).


That is the problem.

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] phylo.modularity
parts:
If one has interspecific data, then non-phylogenetic analyses of modularity or integration are not recommended.

 

As for PICs, they may be used in comparative analyses. However, be aware that any approaches using permutations must be done on the correct exchangeable units. Using permutations of PICs can get one into trouble, as shown in that 2015 paper.


The alternative is phylogenetic transformation + RRPP, which is what our procedures utilize. Phylogenetic transformation yields identical parameter estimates to those found from PICs or PGLS, but has the advantage of having residuals that are the correct exchangeable units under the null hypothesis for the test (see Adams and Collyer, 2018: Evolution on phylogenetic ANOVA).

Dean

parts: Great, thank you very much Dean.
On 27. May 2020, at 21:37, Adams, Dean [EEOB] <dca...@iastate.edu> wrote:

If one has interspecific data, then non-phylogenetic analyses of modularity or integration are not recommended.
 
As for PICs, they may be used in comparative analyses. However, be aware that any approaches using permutations must be done on the correct exchangeable units. Using permutations of PICs can get one into trouble, as shown in that 2015 paper.

The alternative is phylogenetic transformation + RRPP, which is what our procedures utilize. Phylogenetic transformation yields identical parameter estimates to those found from PICs or PGLS, but has the advantage of having residuals that are the correct exchangeable units under the null hypothesis for the test (see Adams and Collyer, 2018: Evolution on phylogenetic ANOVA).

Dean

Ok thanks, that’s not a paper I had seen. Seems to address the point.
To be clear, the permutations referred to in this case would be the iterations performed by the modularity.test function?
 
Then I take it that applying PIC to landmark matrices is generally not recommended, nor is using non-phylogenetic tests of modularity and integration (particularly given how starkly different the results can be). Is that a fair assessment?
 
On 27. May 2020, at 17:23, Adams, Dean [EEOB] <dca...@iastate.edu> wrote:
 
See Adams and Collyer 2015 Evolution (the ‘what you shuffles matters’ paper). Shuffling PICs is not correct for linear models, and is correct here. They are not the correct exchangeable units under the null hypothesis (see Commanges 2003 for general comments on exchangeability for permutation tests).

That is the problem.

Dean

Thanks for the response, but I’m aware of PCMs, and my question was more specifically about the phylo.modularity function.
 
Let me try this a different way: why might the results using phylo.modularity differ significantly from an approach using PIC?
 
Below is an example using the attached testdata.Rdata file. Results for non-phylogenetic and PIC of landmark data are similar (modularity present, p=0.001) while the phylo.modularity test indicates it is not (p=1, CR>1).
 
Adams & Felice 2014 discusses some differences between PIC vs PGLS evolutionary covariance matrix approaches, but can this produce such different results on the same dataset?
Perhaps I’m missing something obvious here…?
 
Thanks again.
 
##
library(geomorph)
library(ape)
 
coords.test <- test.data$coords.test #53 3D landmarks, 10 species
partitions <- test.data$partitions #partition scheme with 6 modules
tree <- test.data$tree
 
# Non-phylogenetic modularity test
non.ph.mod <- modularity.test(coords.test, partition.gp=partitions)
 
# Phylogenetic modularity test
ph.mod <- phylo.modularity(coords.test, partition.gp=partitions, phy=tree, CI = FALSE, iter=499)
 
# PIC modularity test
coords.2d <- two.d.array(coords.test)
pic.mat <- apply(coords.2d, 2, pic, phy=tree) #PIC landmark matrix
pic.mat <- arrayspecs(pic.mat, 53,3)
pic.mod <- modularity.test(pic.mat, partition.gp=partitions)
 
# Compare results
cbind(non.ph.mod, pic.mod, ph.mod)
 
##

On 26. May 2020, at 23:39, Adams, Dean [EEOB] <dca...@iastate.edu> wrote:
 
If I can rephrase your question, you are asking why you have one result when ignoring phylogenetic nonindependence and get a different result when phylogeny is taken into account.  This can happen, and is particularly acute in datasets where interspecific trends also covary with phylogenetic relatedness. When this happens, phylogeny has confounded the signal, and an analysis ignoring phylogeny is incorrect.
 
I suggest a careful reading of the basic statistical literature on phylogenetic comparative methods, starting with Felsenstein 1985 (Am Nat). Recent reviews of PCMs for morphometric data (e.g., Adams and Collyer 2019: Ann. Rev.; 2018: Syst. Biol.) have additional references.

Subject: [geomorph-r-package] phylo.modularity
 
Hi all
I have a dataset of 53 cranial landmarks of mammalian crania on which I'm testing 5 different possible modularity schemes.
Using the regular modularity.test indicates that all 5 schemes are significantly different from null (p = 0.001), with CR values between 0.66 and 0.82, and Z values ranging from -3 to -6. Presumably the scheme with the most negative Z score is preferred.
 
However using the phylo.modularity function indicates that none of these 5 schemes are significant (p ranging from 0.08 to 1), with CR values 0.92 to 1.35, and Z values from -1.5 to +5.5
 
The differences in result are quite striking, but I'm not sure how to interpret this. It's often the case that comparisons within a phylogenetic context are to be preferred, but I can't find examples of others using this specific phylogenetic modularity test.
 
I also tried running modularity.test on the phylogenetically independent contrasts of my procrustes-transformed landmark dataset. The results are closer to the non-phylogenetic modularity test (and this makes sense to me).
 
Any thoughts on why the phylo.modularity function produces such different results than a PIC approach?
 
Thanks
 
Faysal
